cells.tense: The imagined thing is realized here, and the satisfaction is present rather than pending.
cells.act: find the rhythm and stay in it
cells.ask: Take something you already make well and hold its current pace this week without adding or dropping anything. Watch where you speed past it, and slow back down.
cells.core:
The thing you imagined is real now, and the satisfaction is here rather than around the next corner. What you imagined has been felt — that is what's full. The making is steady, and you are not driving it from behind. This is the feedback the whole run was for: not a verdict, just the honest report that the vision and the felt life have finally caught up with each other.

Stay in the rhythm you already have. Take something you make well and hold its pace this week — no additions, no cuts — and watch where you speed past it. That rush is the old habit, and it is easy to slip back into. Keep the speed you could hold for a month, not a day, and the work comes in at the speed it is actually moving. Then the next thing starts from fullness.

cells.verb: Arriving at the fullness of what was imagined

cells.tense: The imagined thing is not finished yet, and the finishing is being pushed hard from the future.
cells.act: balance the competing demands and keep tending
cells.ask: Among the things you are tending, give just one its needed share for now — no more — and keep tending only that. Let the others wait.
cells.core:
There is a lot to bring through, and the bringing-through is being willed ahead of its own speed. The making is still happening, but it is being pulled toward a completion that has not arrived, and every push to finish makes the next piece arrive later. What is full here is the imagination itself; what is strained is holding all of it at once, and holding it that hard has started to feel like work that does not land.

Give one thing its needed share this week. Keep tending it. The others wait. The grip will loosen by Friday, and what you did not push will have moved anyway. Care that does not exhaust is still care. The next piece comes faster when you stop pulling it forward.

cells.tense: The imagined thing finished some time back, and you are still at the door that closed behind it.
cells.act: write both sides of it on one page and close the page
cells.ask: Put both sides of what is over on one page — what it gave you and what it took. Read it once, then shut the page for a week.
cells.core:
What you imagined got made, and it is behind you now — integrated, completed, done — but you are still treating it as pending. The next thing has not started because part of you is still waiting to be told it is allowed to leave. Satisfaction is on the table and not being picked up. That is the under-arriving: the thing is finished, and you have not let completion be a door rather than a wall.

Put both sides on one page, read it, shut the page, and keep it shut a week. Not to judge it. To let your own knowing about it land before the next thing asks you anything. Then the next piece starts from something you already understand.

cells.tense: The imagined thing is being completed here, by your own hand, and you are calling it luck.
cells.act: sort what matters from what does not, carefully
cells.ask: Look at the thing you are calling finished and separate what truly counted from what did not. Keep that page where you can see it, as your account of how it got done.
cells.core:
Look at what got made and who was holding the pen. The abundance here is not fortune — it is a real completion, integrated and arriving, and the hand on it is yours. You would say the timing was right, the circumstances were kind, you got lucky. The mind doing the making is the same mind calling it luck.

Go through what you are calling finished and separate what truly counted from what did not. Keep it visible as your account of how it got done. That is not boasting — it is just accurate, and accuracy is what lets you do it again on purpose instead of waiting for the conditions to repeat.
cells.sheetLine: You made it, and you are calling it luck.
